hints: Think of an experiment where light hitting a metal surface ejects electrons instantly, which wave theory cannot explain by spreading energy continuously.
walkthrough:
**Link Particle Behaviour To Light**
Think of light as arriving in tiny packets of energy called photons. Only a particle model can explain why electrons are emitted instantly when the frequency is above a threshold, and why intensity only changes the number emitted, not their energy.

hints: Think of the opposite case - an experiment where a beam of particles such as electrons passes through a thin crystal and forms an interference pattern, which only waves can do.
walkthrough:
**Link Wave Behaviour To Matter**
Particles like electrons are normally thought of as tiny balls. But when a beam of electrons passes through graphite, it diffracts and forms rings on a screen. Diffraction and interference are wave-only behaviours, so this proves matter can act as a wave.

hints: Recall how the effective wavelength of a matter particle gets smaller when its momentum gets larger - focus on the inverse relationship between $\lambda$ and $p$.
Remember the universal constant that links the particle world to the wave world in this equation, with value $6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$.
walkthrough:
**Recall The Matter-Wave Equation**
For any moving matter particle, its wave-like wavelength is inversely proportional to its momentum: $$\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$$ Larger momentum means shorter wavelength.

**Identify The Symbols**
Here $\lambda$ is the effective wavelength, $p$ is the momentum of the particle, and $h$ is the Planck constant.
Final answer: $\lambda = h/p$, where $h$ is the Planck constant.

hints: Think of the French physicist whose name is given to the idea that every moving particle has an associated wavelength $\lambda = h/p$.
walkthrough:
**Name The Matter Wavelength**
The wavelength associated with a moving particle by $$\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$$ is called the de Broglie wavelength, after Louis de Broglie who proposed matter waves.

hints: Start from energy conservation - the electron starts from rest, so all the electrical work done on it becomes kinetic energy. Think about how to write both energies.
Rearrange to make $v$ the subject and check your units: convert $4.8 \text{ kV}$ to volts and use $m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$ and $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
walkthrough:
**Apply Conservation Of Energy**
An electron accelerated from rest gains kinetic energy equal to the work done by the field: $$eV = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ where $e$ is elementary charge, $V$ is p.d., $m$ is electron mass and $v$ is final speed.

**Substitute And Show The Result**
Rearrange for $v$: $$v = \sqrt{\frac{2eV}{m}}$$ Put in $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $V = 4800 \text{ V}$, $m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$: $$v = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 4800}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}} = 4.1 \times 10^7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$ This matches the value to be shown.

hints: Use the matter-wave equation from (b)(i) and write momentum $p$ in terms of mass and the speed found in (c)(i).
Substitute $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$, $m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$ and $v = 4.1 \times 10^7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, then evaluate for $\lambda$ in metres.
walkthrough:
**Calculate Momentum Then Wavelength**
Use de Broglie equation with $p = mv$: $$\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$$ This shows faster, heavier particles have shorter wavelengths.
